chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from one of his companions, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad, who said:
Is'haq ibn Umar bequeathed at the time of his death regarding his slave-girl singers that we should sell them and carry their price to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him).

Ibrahim said: So I sold the slave-girls for three hundred thousand dirhams and carried the price to him. I said to him: Indeed, a mawla of yours, called Is'haq ibn Umar, has bequeathed at the time of his death the selling of his slave-girl singers and carrying the price to you. I have sold them, and this price is three hundred thousand dirhams.

He (peace be upon him) said: I have no need for it. Indeed, this is ill-gotten gain (suh't). Teaching them is disbelief (kufr), and listening to them is hypocrisy (nifaq), and their price is ill-gotten gain (suh't).
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the earnings of female singers in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Ibrahim ibn Abi al-Bilad conveys the verdict of Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) regarding the wealth derived from female singers, declaring it *suh't* (ill-gotten gain). The Imam provides a tripartite theological classification: teaching them constitutes *kufr* (disbelief), listening to them is *nifaq* (hypocrisy), and their earnings are *suh't*, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on the spiritual impurity of their art and its impact on the listener's faith. This ruling underscores the broader principle that the source of income is intrinsically linked to the nature of the activity itself.
